newsitem.title: FRANCE: New political force emerges in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: New political force emerges in Algeria.

text.p: A new political party close to President Liamine Zeroual is quickly emerging as one of the front-runners in parliamentary elections set for June 5, political analysts said on Wednesday.

Zeroual, a retired general, sees the election as a way of bringing the North African country out of a guerrilla war in which about 60,000 people have died. Fundamentalist Moslem fighters are struggling to overthrow the government.

Algeria has been without an elected parliament for the past five years. The party that proved itself the most powerful in the last, aborted election in 1991, the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), is outlawed and so cannot run. The authorities scrapped the 1991 poll when the radical FIS took a huge lead.

The National Liberation Front (FLN), which ruled in a one-party system after independence in 1962 until reforms brought multi-party elections in 1991, had hoped to win back its political clout in the forthcoming poll.
But analysts said the FLN could be the biggest loser from the formation of the new party, the National Democratic Rally, known by its French initials RND.
"Since the creation of the National Democratic Rally, many political parties believe the government will help this new party to win the majority in the next elections.
"This uneasiness is shared by the National Liberation Front (FLN) which is certainly the big loser," the Algerian newspaper La Tribune wrote on Wednesday.
After talks with Zeroual on Tuesday, which were continuing on Wednesday, party leaders said he had reassured them that Moslem guerrillas could not disrupt the poll.
To guard voters, the government deployed more than 200,000 security forces members in a presidential election in 1995 and in a referendum to change the constitution in 1996.
Political concern is now especially focused on the intentions of the authorities.
Mahfoud Nahnah, leader of the main legal Islamist Hamas party, scorned the authorities for hastily forming the RND, saying the aim was to smother opposition parties.

"We deplore that the new party is engineered to be the ruling party to prevent other political parties from playing their roles," said Nahnah, who gained one third of the 1995 presidential poll which confirmed Zeroual in power.
Abdelkader Bensalah, president of the government-appointed Transitional National Council, formed the RND as the party grouping supporters of Zeroual.

The move dashed hopes nurtured by senior FLN leaders to revive their flagging political fortunes. The FLN changed its leadership last year and moved closer to Zeroual, hoping to enjoy power once more.

"The advent of the RND in the political field has changed fundamentally the political debate creating a climate of doubt and disillusion among almost all political parties," said the influential El Watan newspaper on Wednesday.

A spokesman for the legal Moslem fundamentalist Nahda party said on Wednesday by telephone from Algiers that his party had evidence that some local authorities had told people to vote for the RND, backing their calls by barely veiled threats.
The spokesman said his party had written to the presidency.
The main secular Socialist Forces Front (FFS), whose leader Hocine Ait Ahmed termed the RND "party of the new dictatorship", said the RND had enlisted state servants and clerks.

"This to say that in one hand, the administration goes into the service of the president's party and on the other hand the authorities lock up the (opposition) media...," said FFS leader Seddik Dbaili.
